docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: 1.1 Dataset Origin
docs.text: The Cleveland Heart Disease dataset was collected by Dr. Robert Detrano at the Cleveland Clinic Foundation. It is one of the most widely used datasets in medical machine learning research. The dataset contains 303 patient records with 13 clinical features and 1 target variable.

docs.title: 1.2 Feature-by-Feature Explanation
docs.text: # Feature Type Description Values / Range 1 age Numerical (Continuous) Age of the patient in years. Older patients have higher cardiovascular risk. 29–77 years 2 sex Categorical (Binary) Biological sex of the patient. Males have statistically higher heart disease risk. 0 = Female, 1 = Male 3 cp Categorical (Nominal) Type of chest pain experienced. Asymptomatic chest pain (type 4) is paradoxically the most dangerous indicator. 1 = Typical Angina, 2 = Atypical Angina, 3 = Non-anginal Pain, 4 = Asymptomatic 4 trestbps Numerical (Continuous) Resting blood pressure measured in mm Hg upon hospital admission. Values above 140 indicate hypertension. 94–200 mm Hg 5 chol Numerical (Continuous) Serum cholesterol level in mg/dl. High values (>240) increase coronary artery disease risk. 126–564 mg/dl 6 fbs Categorical (Binary) Whether fasting blood sugar exceeds 120 mg/dl. Elevated fasting glucose suggests diabetes, a heart disease risk factor. 0 = False (≤120), 1 = True (>120) 7 restecg Categorical (Nominal) Resting electrocardiographic results. ST-T abnormalities and left ventricular hypertrophy are pathological signs. 0 = Normal, 1 = ST-T Wave Abnormality, 2 = Left Ventricular Hypertrophy 8 thalach Numerical (Continuous) Maximum heart rate achieved during exercise stress testing. Lower max heart rate correlates with disease. 71–202 bpm 9 exang Categorical (Binary) Whether the patient experiences angina (chest pain) during exercise. Exercise-induced angina is a strong disease predictor. 0 = No, 1 = Yes 10 oldpeak Numerical (Continuous) ST depression induced by exercise relative to rest. Measured from the ECG. Higher values indicate more severe ischemia. 0.0–6.2 11 slope Categorical (Ordinal) Slope of the peak exercise ST segment. A flat or downsloping segment suggests ischemia. 1 = Upsloping, 2 = Flat, 3 = Downsloping 12 ca Categorical (Ordinal) Number of major coronary vessels colored by fluoroscopy. More colored vessels = higher disease severity. Has 4 missing values. 0, 1, 2, 3 13 thal Categorical (Nominal) Thalassemia blood disorder status determined via thallium stress test. Reversible defects are strong disease indicators. Has 2 missing values. 3 = Normal, 6 = Fixed Defect, 7 = Reversible Defect 14 target Target Variable Angiographic diagnosis of heart disease. Original values 1–4 represent disease severity; we binarize to 0 vs 1. 0 = Normal (<50% diameter narrowing), 1 = Heart Disease (≥50% narrowing)

docs.title: 1.3 Identifying Categorical vs. Numerical Columns
docs.text:
In our code (main.py, lines 161–162), we define:

numerical_cols = ['age', 'trestbps', 'chol', 'thalach', 'oldpeak']       # 5 continuous features
categorical_cols = ['sex', 'cp', 'fbs', 'restecg', 'exang', 'slope', 'ca', 'thal']  # 8 categorical features

Why this matters: Numerical columns need scaling (StandardScaler), while categorical columns need encoding (one-hot encoding). Treating categorical variables as numbers would imply false ordinal relationships (e.g., chest pain type 4 is NOT "more than" type 1 — they are different categories).

docs.title: 1.4 Dataset Limitations
docs.text:
1. Extremely Small Sample Size (~300 records): Deep learning models typically need thousands or millions of samples. With only 303 records, the model is prone to overfitting — memorizing the training data instead of learning general patterns.

  2. Missing Values: The ca column has 4 missing entries and thal has 2 missing entries, represented as empty strings or ? in the CSV. These must be imputed before model training.

  3. Single-Center Bias: All data comes from the Cleveland Clinic. Patients from other regions, ethnicities, or socioeconomic backgrounds may have different clinical presentations, limiting the model's generalizability.

  4. Class Imbalance: The dataset has approximately 138 patients with heart disease (target=1) and 165 normal patients (target=0). This mild imbalance (~45:55 ratio) can bias the model toward predicting the majority class.

  5. Feature Limitations: Only 13 clinical features are available. Modern cardiology uses many additional markers (e.g., troponin levels, BNP, CRP, family history, smoking status) that are absent here.

docs.title: 1.5 Why 2D GAF and CNN-LSTM-Attention Can Be Applied to Tabular Data
docs.text:
This is a critical question for your B.Tech viva/defense. Tabular data has no inherent spatial structure (like images) or temporal sequence (like text/audio). So why use a 2D CNN and LSTM?

The key insight: 1. Gramian Angular Fields (GAF): We transform each patient's 28-feature 1D representation into a \(28 imes 28\) correlation image showing how every feature interacts with every other feature. This creates a spatial texture (e.g., cross-diagonal lines) that 2D CNN filters can easily learn. 2. Feature sequence preservation: In our architecture, the 2D CNN slides filters over the image. By pooling across the width dimension (size (1, 28)) and reshaping back to a sequence of (28, filters), the sequence length is preserved. 3. Sequence Modeling & Attention: This allows the Bidirectional LSTM and Attention layers to run on the 28-step sequence, capturing bidirectional dependencies and highlighting important clinical features just as they would on a 1D sequence!

Component Role on Tabular GAF Data 2D GAF (GASF) Encodes the patient's 1D vector into a \(28 imes 28\) image of feature-feature correlation patterns. Conv2D Slides a 2D kernel across the GAF image, extracting spatial textures and local interactions. MaxPooling2D (1, 28) Collapses the width dimension, converting 2D spatial features back to a 28-step sequence. LSTM Models bidirectional dependencies across the 28-step sequence of feature representations. Attention Computes importance weights for each of the 28 features to identify the primary diagnostic drivers.

Research justification: Several peer-reviewed papers (Shickel et al. 2018, Rajkomar et al. 2018) have shown that deep learning architectures originally designed for sequences can effectively model tabular clinical data by capturing non-linear feature interactions that traditional ML methods (logistic regression, random forests) miss.

docs.title: 3. Data Preprocessing
docs.text: All preprocessing is implemented in src/preprocessing.py.

docs.title: 3.1 Missing Value Handling
docs.text:
File: preprocessing.py, load_and_clean_data() function (lines 6–31)

# Step 1: Convert string '?' and empty strings to NaN
for col in df.columns:
    if df[col].dtype == 'object':
        df[col] = df[col].astype(str).str.strip()
        df[col] = df[col].replace({'?': np.nan, '': np.nan})
        df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce')

# Step 2: Impute missing values with column median
for col in df.columns:
    if df[col].isnull().any():
        median_val = df[col].median()
        df[col] = df[col].fillna(median_val)

Why median imputation? - Robust to outliers: Unlike mean, the median is not affected by extreme values (e.g., a cholesterol of 564 mg/dl won't skew the imputed value) - Preserves data distribution: The median maintains the central tendency of the feature - Appropriate for small datasets: More sophisticated methods (KNN imputation, MICE) require more data to work reliably

docs.title: 3.2 Outlier Handling
docs.text:
File: preprocessing.py, cap_outliers_iqr() function (lines 33–46)

def cap_outliers_iqr(df, numerical_cols, factor=1.5):
    df_capped = df.copy()
    for col in numerical_cols:
        Q1 = df_capped[col].quantile(0.25)    # 25th percentile
        Q3 = df_capped[col].quantile(0.75)    # 75th percentile
        IQR = Q3 - Q1                          # Interquartile range
        lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR          # Lower fence
        upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR          # Upper fence
        df_capped[col] = np.clip(df_capped[col], lower_bound, upper_bound)
    return df_capped

How IQR capping works: 

                    Q1        Q3
                    |---------|
        |-----------IQR-------|

Lower Fence = Q1 - 1.5 × IQR    Upper Fence = Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
        ↓                                      ↓
Values below this are capped UP    Values above this are capped DOWN

Why capping instead of removal? With only 303 records, removing outlier rows would further reduce our already tiny dataset. Capping (winsorization) preserves the sample while limiting the influence of extreme values on neural network training.

docs.title: 3.4 Feature Scaling
docs.text:
File: preprocessing.py, lines 65–68

scaler = StandardScaler()
scaled_numerical = scaler.fit_transform(df_capped[numerical_cols])

StandardScaler formula (applied to each numerical feature):

X_scaled = (X - μ) / σ

Where μ is the mean and σ is the standard deviation. This transforms each feature to have mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1.

Why scaling is critical for neural networks: - Without scaling, features with large ranges (e.g., cholesterol: 126–564) would dominate features with small ranges (e.g., oldpeak: 0–6.2) - Neural network gradients would be dominated by large-valued features, leading to unstable training - Batch Normalization helps but does not fully replace input scaling

docs.title: 3.5 Train-Validation-Test Split
docs.text:
File: preprocessing.py, lines 96–104

# Step 1: Split off 20% for Test (stratified)
X_train_val, X_test, y_train_val, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_processed, y, test_size=0.20, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

# Step 2: Split remaining into 70% Train and 10% Validation (12.5% of remaining)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_train_val, y_train_val, test_size=0.125, stratify=y_train_val, random_state=42
)

Split ratios: 70% Train (~212 samples) / 10% Validation (~30 samples) / 20% Test (~61 samples)

Why three splits? - Training set: Model learns weights from this data - Validation set: Used during training for EarlyStopping and ReduceLROnPlateau decisions — the model never learns from this - Test set: Used ONLY at the very end to report final, unbiased metrics. The model never sees this during training or hyperparameter selection

docs.title: 3.6 Stratified Splitting
docs.text:
The stratify=y parameter ensures that each split maintains the same class ratio as the original dataset: 

Original:    54.5% Normal, 45.5% Disease
Training:    ~54.5% Normal, ~45.5% Disease  ✓ Same ratio preserved
Validation:  ~54.5% Normal, ~45.5% Disease  ✓ Same ratio preserved
Test:        ~54.5% Normal, ~45.5% Disease  ✓ Same ratio preserved

Without stratification, a random split on such a small dataset could accidentally create a test set with 80% disease patients, giving misleading results.

docs.title: 3.7 SMOTE Implementation
docs.text:
File: preprocessing.py, lines 108–118

from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
smote = SMOTE(random_state=42)
X_train_arr, y_train_arr = smote.fit_resample(X_train.values, y_train.values)

How SMOTE works: 1. For each minority class sample, find its K nearest neighbors (default K=5) 2. Randomly select one of the K neighbors 3. Create a synthetic sample at a random point on the line between the original sample and the selected neighbor: 

X_synthetic = X_original + random(0,1) × (X_neighbor - X_original)
4. Repeat until the minority class has as many samples as the majority class

Critical rule: SMOTE is applied only to the training set, never to validation or test sets. Applying SMOTE before splitting would leak synthetic information into the test set, producing artificially inflated metrics.

Our output: SMOTE applied: Training set shape increased from 211 to 228.

feature_mapping = {}

# Numerical features: direct 1:1 mapping

This mapping is essential for explainability. When we compute Grad-CAM or Attention weights on the 28-feature one-hot encoded input, we need to aggregate those weights back to the original 13 clinical features for meaningful interpretation.

docs.title: 3.9 1D-to-2D Image Conversion (Gramian Angular Fields - GAF)
docs.text:
To prepare our scaled, one-hot encoded patient representations for the 2D CNN, we perform the following transformations:

  1. Polar Coordinates Mapping: Each feature \(\tilde{x}_i \in [-1, 1]\) is converted to a polar angle: $\(\phi_i = \arccos(\tilde{x}_i)\)$

  2. Gramian Angular Summation Field (GASF): We construct a correlation matrix where each cell represents the trigonometric summation of the angles between feature \(i\) and feature \(j\): $\(GASF_{i,j} = \cos(\phi_i + \phi_j) = \tilde{x}_i \tilde{x}_j - \sqrt{1 - \tilde{x}_i^2} \sqrt{1 - \tilde{x}_j^2}\)$ This results in a \(28 \times 28 \times 1\) image (grayscale) representing the complete correlation structure, where each pixel represents the correlation and interaction between two clinical features.

docs.title: 4.1 Why Conv2D is Used (Using GASF Image Input)
docs.text:
By transforming the tabular data into a 2D Gramian Angular Summation Field (GASF) image, we can use 2D Convolutional layers (Conv2D).

Conv2D operation: A 2D kernel of size \(K imes K\) slides across both the height and width of the \(28 imes 28\) feature image:

GASF Input:  28 x 28 correlation grid
Kernel:      K x K (we use 3x3 or 5x5 filters)

Mathematical formula:

\[Z(i, j, c_{out}) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \sum_{l=0}^{K-1} \sum_{m=0}^{C_{in}-1} W(k, l, m, c_{out}) imes X(i+k, j+l, m) + b(c_{out})\]

Where: - H, W = height and width of the image (28x28) - K = kernel size (e.g., 3) - C_in = input channels (1, grayscale GASF image) - C_out = number of filters (we use 32)

What Conv2D learns on GAF data: It learns spatial feature-feature correlation patterns. Instead of just analyzing adjacent features linearly, the 2D filters identify cross-features correlation signatures across the entire grid.

docs.title: 4.2 Why LSTM Is Used
docs.text:
A standard LSTM processes the sequence left-to-right only. A Bidirectional LSTM (LSTM) processes it in both directions:

Forward LSTM:   age → sex → cp → trestbps → chol → ... → thal  →  h_forward
Backward LSTM:  thal → ... → chol → trestbps → cp → sex → age  →  h_backward

Combined output: h_t = [h_forward_t ; h_backward_t]  (concatenated)

LSTM gate equations (computed at each time step t):

Forget gate:    f_t = σ(W_f × x_t + U_f × h_{t-1} + b_f)
Input gate:     i_t = σ(W_i × x_t + U_i × h_{t-1} + b_i)
Cell candidate: c̃_t = tanh(W_c × x_t + U_c × h_{t-1} + b_c)
Cell state:     c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c̃_t
Output gate:    o_t = σ(W_o × x_t + U_o × h_{t-1} + b_o)
Hidden state:   h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t)

Where: - σ = sigmoid activation (outputs 0–1, acting as a "gate") - ⊙ = element-wise multiplication - W, U = learnable weight matrices - b = bias vectors

Why LSTM for tabular data: Since feature ordering in tabular data is arbitrary, processing features in both directions ensures the model captures interactions regardless of order. The forward pass might learn age → sex → cp interactions while the backward pass captures thal → ca → slope interactions.

docs.title: 4.3 The Attention Mechanism
docs.text:
The problem Attention solves: After the LSTM, we have hidden states h_1, h_2, ..., h_T — one for each feature step. We need to condense these T vectors into a single vector for classification. Options: 1. Use only the last hidden state (h_T) — ignores information from earlier steps 2. Average all hidden states — treats all features equally (which is incorrect; some features matter more) 3. Use Attention ✓ — learns which features to focus on

Attention mathematics (implemented in our TabularAttention class):

Step 1 - Projection:      u_t = tanh(W_w × h_t + b_w)
Step 2 - Score:            s_t = u_t^T × u_w
Step 3 - Softmax:          α_t = exp(s_t) / Σ_i exp(s_i)
Step 4 - Context vector:   v = Σ_t α_t × h_t

Where: - h_t = LSTM hidden state at feature step t (shape: 2D, since LSTM concatenates forward+backward) - W_w = learnable projection matrix (shape: 2D × 2D) - b_w = learnable bias (shape: 2D) - u_w = learnable context query vector (shape: 2D) — represents "what does the ideal important feature look like?" - α_t = attention weight for feature step t (between 0 and 1, all weights sum to 1) - v = final patient representation, a weighted combination of all feature representations

Clinical interpretation: The attention weight α_t tells us how important feature t was for the model's prediction. If α_ca = 0.25 and α_chol = 0.03, the model considers ca (vessel count) 8× more important than chol (cholesterol) for this patient.

docs.title: 4.4 Input Reshaping
docs.text:
File: preprocessing.py, lines 120–123

# Original tabular data: (N_samples, N_features) e.g., (211, 28)
# Reshaped for Conv1D:   (N_samples, N_features, 1) e.g., (211, 28, 1)

X_train_reshaped = batch_compute_gasf(X_train_arr)

Why convert to GAF shapes?

Conv2D expects inputs of shape (batch_size, height, width, channels): - batch_size = number of patients in a batch - height, width = dimensions of GAF image = 28 x 28 - channels = channels = 1 (grayscale image representing pairwise angles summation correlation).

This is analogous to converting a 1D signal to a 2D image representation.

docs.title: 5. 2D CNN Model
docs.text: File: src/models.py, build_cnn() function (lines 66–99)

docs.title: 5.1 Architecture Diagram
docs.text:
Input (28, 28, 1)  [GAF Image]
    ↓
Conv2D (32 filters, kernel_size=3, padding='same', L2 regularization)
    ↓
BatchNormalization
    ↓
ReLU Activation
    ↓
MaxPooling2D (pool_size=(1, 28))  [Collapses width to sequence]
    ↓
Flatten
    ↓

    ↓

docs.title: 5.2 Layer-by-Layer Explanation
docs.text:
Layer 1 — Input: layers.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1)) - Defines the expected input shape. Each patient is represented by a \(28 imes 28\) single-channel GAF correlation image.

Layer 2 — Conv2D: layers.Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=(3, 3), padding='same') - 32 filters: The layer learns 32 spatial correlation filter kernels. - kernel_size=(3, 3): Each filter looks at a local \(3 imes 3\) feature correlation window. - padding='same': Keeps the spatial dimensions at \(28 imes 28\) through zero padding. - L2 regularization (1e-4): Penalizes large weights to mitigate overfitting. - Output shape: (batch, 28, 28, 32)

Layer 3 — BatchNormalization: - Normalizes the activations across the batch to have mean ≈ 0 and variance ≈ 1 - Why: Stabilizes training, allows higher learning rates, and acts as a mild regularizer - Mathematically: y = γ × (x - μ_batch) / √(σ²_batch + ε) + β

Layer 4 — ReLU: max(0, x) - Introduces non-linearity. Without activation functions, stacking linear layers would still produce a linear model. - Why ReLU over sigmoid/tanh: ReLU avoids the vanishing gradient problem and is computationally efficient.

Layer 5 — MaxPooling2D: pool_size=(1, 28) - Pools across the width dimension (size 28) to compress spatial features back into a 1D sequence of length 28 (shape: batch × 28 × 1 × filters) - Allows subsequent layers to receive sequential data steps corresponding to the original features.

Layer 6 — Flatten: Converts the 3D tensor (batch, 28, 32) → 2D tensor (batch, 896)

Layer 7 — Dropout (0.3): Randomly sets 30% of neuron outputs to 0 during training - Purpose: Prevents co-adaptation of neurons (a form of overfitting). Forces the network to learn redundant representations.

Layer 8 — Dense (16, ReLU): Fully connected layer with 16 neurons - Learns a compressed representation of the extracted features for classification

Layer 9 — Dense (1, Sigmoid): Output layer - Sigmoid activation: σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-x)) - Outputs a probability between 0 and 1: probability of heart disease - If output ≥ 0.5 → predicted as Heart Disease, else Normal

docs.title: 7.2 The Custom TabularAttention Layer
docs.text:
File: src/models.py, TabularAttention class (lines 4–64)

@tf.keras.utils.register_keras_serializable()
class TabularAttention(layers.Layer):

Why @register_keras_serializable()? This decorator allows the custom layer to be properly serialized/deserialized when saving and loading models. Without it, model.save() and model.load_weights() would fail.

The build() method (called once, when the layer first receives input):

def build(self, input_shape):
    D = input_shape[-1]  # Hidden dimension (64 for LSTM with 32 units)

    # Projection weight matrix: (64, 64)
    self.W = self.add_weight(name="attention_weights_proj", shape=(D, D), ...)

    # Projection bias: (64,)
    self.b = self.add_weight(name="attention_bias_proj", shape=(D,), ...)

    # Context query vector: (64, 1) — the "ideal feature" that the model learns
    self.u = self.add_weight(name="attention_query_vector", shape=(D, 1), ...)

The call() method (executed on every forward pass):

def call(self, inputs):  # inputs shape: (batch, 28, 64)

    # Step 1: Project each hidden state through a tanh activation
    u_t = tf.tanh(tf.tensordot(inputs, self.W, axes=1) + self.b)
    # u_t shape: (batch, 28, 64)

    # Step 2: Compute similarity score with the context query vector
    scores = tf.tensordot(u_t, self.u, axes=1)
    # scores shape: (batch, 28, 1)

    # Step 3: Normalize scores via softmax → attention weights
    alphas = tf.nn.softmax(scores, axis=1)
    # alphas shape: (batch, 28, 1) — weights sum to 1 across 28 feature steps

    # Step 4: Weighted sum of original hidden states → context vector
    context = tf.reduce_sum(inputs * alphas, axis=1)
    # context shape: (batch, 64) — the final patient representation

    return context, alphas

docs.title: EarlyStopping
docs.text:
tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
    monitor='val_loss',          # Watch validation loss
    patience=15,                 # Stop if no improvement for 15 consecutive epochs
    restore_best_weights=True,   # Revert to the epoch with lowest val_loss
    verbose=1
)

Why: Without EarlyStopping, the model would continue training until the maximum epoch count, likely overfitting. EarlyStopping detects when the model starts memorizing training data (validation loss increases while training loss decreases) and stops training.

docs.title: ReduceLROnPlateau
docs.text:
tf.keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(
    monitor='val_loss',      # Watch validation loss
    factor=0.5,              # Multiply learning rate by 0.5 when triggered
    patience=7,              # Wait 7 epochs of no improvement before reducing
    min_lr=1e-6,             # Never reduce below this value
    verbose=1
)

Why: When training plateaus (validation loss stops decreasing), reducing the learning rate allows the optimizer to make finer adjustments, potentially escaping local minima and finding a better solution.

Learning rate schedule example: 

Epochs 1-15:   lr = 0.001
Epoch 16:      Plateau detected → lr = 0.0005
Epochs 16-23:  lr = 0.0005
Epoch 24:      Plateau detected → lr = 0.00025
...and so on

File: src/train.py, run_cross_validation() function (lines 114–228)

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

How Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation works:

Fold 1: [████████████ Train ████████████] [██ Val ██]
Fold 2: [██████████ Train ██] [██ Val ██] [██ Train ██]
Fold 3: [████████ Train ██] [██ Val ██] [████ Train ████]
Fold 4: [██████ Train ██] [██ Val ██] [██████ Train ██████]
Fold 5: [██ Val ██] [████████████ Train ████████████████]

Critical implementation detail — Data preprocessing happens inside each fold (lines 138–157):

for fold, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(skf.split(X_df, y_series)):
    # 1. Split data for this fold
    # 2. Fit scaler on TRAINING fold only, then transform both
    scaler = StandardScaler()
    X_tr_num_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_tr_raw[numerical_cols])  # fit on train
    X_va_num_scaled = scaler.transform(X_va_raw[numerical_cols])      # transform only on val

    # 3. One-hot encode inside the fold
    # 4. Apply SMOTE only to training fold
    # 5. Train model and evaluate

Why this prevents data leakage: If we scaled or applied SMOTE before splitting, information from validation samples would "leak" into the training process (e.g., the scaler's mean/std would be influenced by validation data). By doing everything inside the fold, each fold is a completely independent experiment.

docs.title: 10.1 Metrics Explained
docs.text: All metrics are computed in src/train.py, train_and_evaluate_holdout() function (lines 94–101):

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

The proportion of all predictions that were correct. Limitation: Can be misleading with class imbalance (a model that always predicts "Normal" would get ~55% accuracy on our dataset).

docs.title: Precision
docs.text:
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)

"Of all patients the model predicted as having heart disease, how many actually had it?" - High precision → few false alarms - Critical in: situations where false positives are costly (unnecessary surgeries)

docs.title: Recall (Sensitivity)
docs.text:
Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

"Of all patients who actually have heart disease, how many did the model correctly identify?" - High recall → few missed diagnoses - Critical in: medical screening where missing a disease case is dangerous

docs.title: F1 Score
docs.text:
F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

The harmonic mean of precision and recall. Provides a single balanced metric when you need both high precision and high recall.

docs.title: ROC-AUC
docs.text: The Receiver Operating Characteristic curve plots True Positive Rate (Recall) vs. False Positive Rate at various classification thresholds. The Area Under the Curve (AUC) summarizes overall discrimination ability: - AUC = 1.0: Perfect classifier - AUC = 0.5: Random guessing (the diagonal line) - AUC < 0.5: Worse than random

These patients were correctly identified, preventing unnecessary medical anxiety and follow-up screening. - False Positives (FP) = 8: Patients who were clinically Normal but predicted by the model as having Heart Disease. docs.title: 11.1 Grad-CAM for 2D GAF Images
docs.text:
Function: compute_grad_cam_2d() (lines 6–51)

Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) is computed on the 2D spatial feature maps of the final Conv2D layer. We then pool/average it to link it back to our 1D clinical features.

Mathematical formulation:

Step 1: Compute gradients of the prediction logit w.r.t. the Conv2D layer output
        ∂y / ∂A^k    where A^k is the k-th filter's 2D activation map (size H x W)

Step 2: Global Average Pooling of the gradients across both dimensions (0, 1, 2)
        α_k = (1 / (H × W)) × Σ_i Σ_j (∂y / ∂A^k_{i,j})

Step 3: Weighted combination + ReLU (creates 2D heatmap)
        L_GradCAM_2D = ReLU(Σ_k α_k × A^k)

Step 4: Average along axis 0 to reduce 2D heatmap to 1D importance vector
        L_GradCAM_1D = mean(L_GradCAM_2D, axis=0)

Implementation detail — using logits instead of probabilities:

# Instead of: loss = predictions (probability)
# We compute: logit = log(p / (1-p))
p = tf.clip_by_value(predictions[:, 0], 1e-7, 1.0 - 1e-7)
logit = tf.math.log(p / (1.0 - p))

Why? When the sigmoid output is close to 0 or 1 (saturated), the gradients become extremely small (vanishing gradients). By computing gradients w.r.t. the logit (before sigmoid), we avoid this issue and get meaningful gradient magnitudes.

docs.title: 11.3 One-Hot to Original Feature Aggregation
docs.text:
Function: aggregate_one_hot_weights() (lines 69–90)

Since our input has 28 one-hot encoded features but clinicians think in terms of the original 13 features, we aggregate:

for i, orig_feat in enumerate(original_features):
    indices = feature_mapping[orig_feat]
    # Sum the weights of all one-hot columns belonging to this original feature
    agg_weights[i] = sum(processed_weights[idx] for idx in indices)

# Normalize so weights sum to 1.0
agg_weights = agg_weights / np.sum(agg_weights)

Grad-CAM weights at these indices: [0.12, 0.08, 0.03, 0.15]
Aggregated weight for 'cp' = 0.12 + 0.08 + 0.03 + 0.15 = 0.38

docs.title: 12.3 Why More Complex ≠ Better (Critical Research Insight)
docs.text:
This is the most important finding for your thesis/viva:

On a dataset of only ~300 samples, adding complexity hurts performance:

  1. Parameter explosion: - CNN: ~15,000 parameters - CNN-LSTM: ~45,000 parameters - CNN-LSTM-Attention: ~55,000+ parameters

With 300 training samples, the parameter-to-sample ratio is dangerously high for complex models.

  1. Overfitting cascade: Each additional layer (LSTM, Attention) adds more parameters that the model can use to memorize training data rather than learning general patterns.

  2. The CNN's advantage: The Conv2D layer's weight sharing (the same kernel is applied at every position) acts as a strong implicit regularizer. It has far fewer parameters per feature interaction compared to a fully connected layer.

  3. When the full architecture shines: With larger datasets (>5,000 samples), the CNN-LSTM-Attention architecture would likely outperform CNN alone because the additional capacity would be used to learn genuine complex interactions rather than memorize noise.

docs.title: 12.4 How to Discuss This in Your Thesis
docs.text: "While the CNN-LSTM-Attention architecture provides superior explainability through its attention mechanism, the ablation study reveals that on small clinical datasets (~300 records), simpler architectures generalize better. The 2D CNN model achieved a cross-validated accuracy of 77.86% and ROC-AUC of 84.67%. The attention mechanism remains valuable for its interpretability — enabling clinicians to understand which clinical features drive individual predictions — even when the overall prediction accuracy is lower. This suggests a trade-off between model complexity, interpretability, and performance that is particularly acute in medical AI applications with limited data."

docs.text: Mistake Consequence Our Solution Applying SMOTE before train-test split Synthetic minority samples leak into the test set, inflating metrics by 5-15% SMOTE applied only to training split Scaling the entire dataset before splitting Test set statistics influence the scaler's mean/std fit_transform on train, transform on val/test Using accuracy alone for evaluation Misleading on imbalanced data (55% accuracy by always predicting "Normal") Report Precision, Recall, F1, ROC-AUC alongside accuracy Not using restore_best_weights=True Model may use weights from a later, overfit epoch EarlyStopping restores best weights automatically Treating categorical features as numerical Implies false ordinal relationships (cp=4 > cp=1) One-hot encoding for all categorical features Computing Grad-CAM on sigmoid output Vanishing gradients when prediction is close to 0 or 1 Use logit-space: log(p / (1-p)) Training one model and reporting its score High variance on small datasets 5-Fold Cross-Validation provides robust estimates

docs.title: 13.3 Research-Level Insights
docs.text:
1. The Bias-Variance Tradeoff on Small Medical Datasets: Our ablation study demonstrates a textbook case — the simplest model (CNN) has the best generalization because it has low variance (consistent across folds), even if it may have higher bias (simpler decision boundary). The complex CNN-LSTM-Attention has low bias but extremely high variance.

  2. Attention as Explanation, Not Just Performance: Even though the Attention model has lower accuracy, the attention weights provide clinically meaningful explanations. In medical AI, a slightly less accurate model that can explain its reasoning is often preferred over a black-box model with marginally higher accuracy.

  3. The Role of Grad-CAM: Grad-CAM provides a complementary view to attention. While attention shows what the model "focuses on" globally, Grad-CAM shows what specifically influenced the gradient flow for a particular prediction. This dual-explanation approach strengthens the trustworthiness of the model.

  4. Practical Recommendation: For deployment on small clinical datasets: - Use the CNN model for prediction accuracy - Use the CNN-LSTM-Attention model for explainability - Present both to clinicians: the CNN prediction with the Attention model's feature importance explanation

docs.text:
This project implements a complete, research-grade pipeline for explainable heart disease prediction:

  6. Clinical interpretability: Feature importance mapped back to the 13 original clinical features

The simpler CNN model generalizes best on this small dataset (80.86% CV accuracy, 88.31% ROC-AUC), while the CNN-LSTM-Attention model provides valuable clinical explainability through attention weights, demonstrating the fundamental trade-off between model complexity and generalization in medical AI.
